Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing knowledge-base entries from a fixed set of cited papers. Each of 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references, 515 papers, 19% readable in full via open access) is written from its header and exactly the papers its curators cited, with the causal gene withheld. Six generation strategies are compared under one model (Claude Opus 5.5), one set of guards, one claim-level audit with a single repair round, and one scoring procedure: direct reading (all papers in one prompt), an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control. Three add-ons and four 'reading better' variants are tested against their parents. The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', scores what a draft says about each cited paper against 6,652 facts split once, before any draft was seen, from OMIM's allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar. Main findings: (i) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a); (ii) the reading strategies convey 91-94% of facts the supplied text is judged to state and under 7% of facts it does not (Fig. 2c); (iii) the agent and the evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading, while the case table trails by 1.9 points (Table 1, Fig. 3a); (iv) on 38 held-out entries a per-paper completeness pass adds 2.6 points (95% CI 1.7 to 3.6) without lowering audited fidelity (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 3b); (v) a planted-error study shows that the best-verdict audit catches citation swaps and single-value substitutions but cannot see added irrelevant citations or omissions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4). Exploratory runs compare released pipelines (PaperQA2 without its agent, GraphRAG, and STORM, which produced nothing), padded inputs and large entries (Sec. 4.4). The same model family generated, audited and judged everything, and no human validated any judgement.
Strengths: Careful controlled design: the model, the papers supplied, the guards, the audit and the scoring are held fixed, and only the strategy varies (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). The paper fixes the papers to the curators' own reference list and manipulates access within papers, which separates the effect of what was read from the effect of how it was read. Prior strategy comparisons (QA, query-focused summarisation) do not do this.

Fact lists are fixed once, before any draft is seen, and reused for every strategy (Sec. 3.3, 'Primary endpoint'). The paper also shows that splitting facts afresh for each draft inflates levels by 2-5 points (Table 5), which is a useful methodological result for long-form evaluation.

Completion is handled with unusual care. The symmetric completion rule, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis that counts a missing draft as zero (Table 10), and an explicit account of how safety-filter stops cost one-call strategies whole entries but per-paper strategies single papers (Sec. 3.3, Table 4) are good practice that most agentic-pipeline comparisons omit.

Paired statistics are reported properly. Each comparison gives a bootstrap CI over entries, better/worse/tied counts, an exact sign test, and Holm adjustment for the secondary measures (Sec. 3.3, Table 7). Replicate noise (three generation, audit and scoring replicates on 30 entries) and judge variation are measured and kept separate from the inferential test (App. E, Table 19).

The split of coverage by whether the supplied text states each fact (Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 3, Table 18) is an informative diagnostic. It shows that the remaining headroom lies mostly in access, not in reading strategy, and it locates the completeness-pass gain on stated facts in full-text papers (Fig. 3b).

The audit stress test is concrete and useful. Because a claim takes the best verdict over its cited papers, none of 30 added irrelevant citations was flagged, even though the added paper's own verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 claims attributed to it (Sec. 4.5, Table 47). This is a clear warning about a common citation-verification design.

Reporting is unusually candid. Negative results (learned guide, reconciliation), deviations from the design (App. J, K, L), exploratory status, and confounds (creation era, development on evaluation entries) are all stated. A memory-only control and a set of 2026 entries chosen by creation date address contamination (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 5, App. M.2). Per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores are to be released.
Weaknesses: No judgement in the study is validated by a person, and the same model family writes, audits, splits facts, judges whether facts are conveyed, and judges whether the supplied text states each fact (Sec. 3.2, Limitation (i)). Every headline number depends on these judgements: the 79.8% vs 36.1% access effect, the 91-94% coverage of stated facts, the null between-strategy differences, and the 2.6-point completeness gain. Judge-variation and replicate figures (App. E) measure the judge's consistency, not its validity. Self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024, cited in Sec. 2) and correlated errors between the 'stated' judge and the 'conveyed' judge could inflate the stated-fact coverage in Fig. 2c in particular. For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark and its measurement lessons, even a modest expert-annotated sample (for example a few hundred fact-status and 'stated' judgements, with agreement statistics) or a second-family judge on a subset is a basic requirement that is missing.

The main comparison does not match settings across paradigms, and this bears directly on the headline claim that no design beat direct reading. Writers run at high reasoning effort, but per-paper extraction in the evidence graph and the case table runs at medium effort, and synopsis terms for those two strategies are computed by rule (Sec. 3.2, App. B). In the matched ablation (Sec. 4.2, App. F) the case table moves from -2.3 to -0.2 points, and the matched evidence graph is above direct reading (+1.8, CI +0.4 to +3.3) on 38 entries. The paper's own measurement lesson is to 'match settings unrelated to the representation before blaming it' (Sec. 5), yet the unmatched configuration is the primary comparison in Table 1 and the abstract.

The regime tested is the one where direct reading is expected to win, and it also leaves little headroom for strategies to differ. Entries have 2-12 references with a median of about 39k characters (Sec. 4.4), and 81% of papers are abstract or title only. On facts stated in abstract-only papers the strategies already convey 95.5-97.1% and most entries tie (Sec. 4.1, Table 18). The differences between strategies are therefore effectively measured on the roughly 40 entries with stated full-text facts (Fig. 3a). The regime where intermediate representations might matter, large sets of relevant papers, produced no comparable entry (0 of 4 large entries; padding used unrelated papers that no draft cited; Sec. 4.4). The conclusion that access matters more than strategy is therefore partly a consequence of the sampling design.

The main 'access bounds agreement' result is close to expected by construction, as the paper itself acknowledges (Sec. 1, line 98). OMIM's allelic-variant descriptions were written from full papers, often including their supplements, so text restricted to abstracts cannot state many of these facts. The stated/not-stated split partly restates this. Its value is the measured size, but that size depends on one model's judgement of what an abstract 'states', and on a reference that covers about 24% of a draft's statements (Limitation (ii), App. H). Because of this narrow, variant-centred reference, recall on it is a partial view of entry quality. A strategy that writes more phenotype or clinical content gets no credit beyond the audit, and draft content outside the reference is checked only for fidelity, not correctness.

Several claims rest on weak or inconsistent inference. (a) The case-table deficit in Table 1 and the abstract has a bootstrap CI that excludes zero, but the sign test gives p = 0.071, the primary endpoint is not adjusted across five comparisons, and under ITT the deficit is -1.4 (-4.2 to +1.4) (Sec. 4.2, Table 10). The stronger evidence, -8.4 points on stated full-text facts, is a restriction to 40 entries, and the paper does not say whether that restriction was specified in advance. (b) The released-pipeline comparison (Sec. 4.4, App. J) uses 10 and 4 entries. PaperQA2 ran without its agent, GraphRAG answered six concatenated section questions (a task-format mismatch), and only the authors' drafts went through repair. It supports little beyond 'not outperformed at these settings'. (c) The reading-better arms lost 3 and 6 of 41 entries to stops while the baseline lost none (Sec. 4.3), and no ITT analysis of those arms is reported in the main text.

The main strategies were developed on the same 100 entries they are evaluated on (Limitation (vi)), which may favour the baseline whose prompt received the most iteration. The held-out checks are small: 20 compared 2026 entries, and the reading-better arms on 38 entries. Memorisation also remains a live confound for the reading strategies. Direct reading's coverage of abstract-only facts falls from 49.8% to 37.9% across creation eras (Sec. 4.2), and the 1.7% 'in no supplied text' estimate rests on the same model judge (Sec. 4.1).

Generality is limited to one proprietary model used through a CLI with no temperature or seed control (Sec. 3.2, Reproducibility statement). Model-dependent safety-filter stops shaped which entries and systems could be compared at all: STORM produced nothing, and 0 of 4 large entries were completed. Results may not transfer to other model families, and an open-weights replication is not provided. At ICLR, findings about strategies for LLM pipelines need at least a second model to support the 'strategy vs access' conclusion.

Technical novelty for an ML venue is modest. The strategies are standard instances of known paradigms, and the 'reading better' interventions are simple prompt-level additions. The contribution is a careful empirical study and a set of measurement lessons in one biomedical curation setting, and its significance for the broader ICLR audience is not argued beyond Sec. 5.

The presentation is very dense and hard to follow. Almost every sentence of Sec. 4 packs several estimates, intervals, entry counts and caveats (for example Sec. 4.1 'Second-hand passages' and Sec. 4.4 'Input size'). Key definitions ('points', pooled vs mean, 'stated', 'judged supported', completion) are spread across Sec. 3.3 and the appendix. The main text interleaves exploratory runs on 4-10 entries with the primary results. The appendix has more than 50 tables, and important design facts, such as the reasoning-effort mismatch, appear only in App. B and F. The title runs four lines. A reader struggles to separate the primary, pre-specified analyses from secondary and post-hoc ones.
Questions: Can you add a human validation of the measurement? For example: domain experts re-judge a stratified sample of fact statuses (present/partly/absent/contradicted), 'stated' availability judgements, and audit verdicts, with agreement statistics (kappa, confusion matrices) per strategy. Does the strategy ordering in Table 1 and Fig. 3a hold under the human labels?

Can you re-judge a subset of drafts with a judge from a different model family, to test for self-preference and for correlated errors between the 'stated' judge and the 'conveyed' judge? In particular, does the 91-94% coverage of stated facts (Fig. 2c) survive a cross-family judge?

Why does the primary comparison run per-paper extraction at medium effort and compute synopsis terms by rule, while writers run at high effort? Given the matched-ablation results (Sec. 4.2, App. F), would you report the matched configuration as the main comparison, ideally on all 93 entries?

Which analyses were pre-specified? In particular, were the restriction to facts stated in full-text papers (where the case table trails by -8.4 points) and the stated/not-stated split defined before the main results were seen?

For the reading-better arms (Sec. 4.3), what are the results under an intention-to-treat analysis, with a stopped entry either scored as zero or falling back to the baseline draft? The completeness arms lost 3 and 6 of 41 entries while the baseline lost none.

How sensitive are the primary endpoint and the between-strategy differences to the half credit for 'partly present'? Table 5 reports 'fully' coverage, but are paired differences under full-credit-only scoring available?

What fraction of the curator facts that the supplied text does not state about full-text papers are likely in supplementary material? Could the supplements of the 96 full-text papers be retrieved, at least for the hidden-full-text experiment, to bound how much of the access effect is supplement-only content?

For the released pipelines, how much of the gap is due to format? Both systems were asked six section questions and the answers were concatenated. Would running direct reading through the same six-question protocol make the comparison more like for like?

Have you tried any strategy on another model family, even on the 30-entry replicate subset? Does the conclusion that access matters more than strategy hold for a weaker or open-weights model, where long-context reading might degrade and structured extraction might help more?
Limitations: The authors list limitations thoroughly (Sec. 5, (i)-(xi)), and the ethics statement addresses clinical misuse and the rights of curated text. Points that deserve more weight or are missing:

The lack of any human validation is presented as a caveat. It is more than that: it limits whether the benchmark can be used as a reference by others, and it should be addressed rather than only acknowledged.

The results come from one proprietary model whose safety filter determined which entries and systems could be compared. This should be stated as a limit on the generality of the central 'access over strategy' conclusion, not only as a completion issue.
The unmatched reasoning-effort configuration of the main comparison should be listed as a limitation of the headline between-strategy result.

The regime choice (small reference lists, mostly abstracts) compresses the measurable differences between strategies. This should be stated as a reason the near-null result may not generalise, beyond the note on large entries.

Licensing: the reference relies on OMIM text deposited in ClinVar. The paper says the text is not redistributed and that rights holders' terms apply, but whether others can rebuild and use the benchmark under those terms should be stated explicitly.
